bib.title: How Well Do Agentic Skills Work in the Wild: Benchmarking LLM Skill Usage in Realistic Settings

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "How Well Do Agentic Skills Work in the Wild: Benchmarking LLM Skill Usage in Realistic Settings", Yujian Liu, Jiabao Ji, Li An, Tommi Jaakkola, Yang Zhang, Shiyu Chang (UCSB, MIT CSAIL, MIT-IBM). Preprint, "Under review" (COLM template), arXiv:2604.04323v1, 6 Apr 2026.

COVERAGE: Read 19 of 19 pages, all ~62.8k chars: body, Tables 1-3, Fig 1-3 data, appendices A-D (search engine, experiment details, refinement prompts, judge prompt). The reference list (pp. 11-13) was skimmed only. No extraction fault. I did not read the target note beyond a grep: it has a skills section at line 203 and a "Writing a skill" section at line 236.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Skill benefit degrades as setups get more realistic, approaching the no-skill baseline in the hardest one.
  number: Claude Opus 4.6 pass rate 55.4 (force-loaded), 51.2 (curated), 43.5 (+distractors), 40.1 (retrieved w/ curated), 38.4 (retrieved w/o curated), 35.4 (no skill)
  setup: SkillsBench, 84 tasks, 3 runs each, Claude Code harness. Retrieved = top-5 from 34,198 real skills.
  quote: "Force-loading curated skills yields 55.4% for Claude, but simply letting the agent decide which to load reduces this to 51.2%, even though the same skills are available. Adding distractors causes a further drop to 43.5%."
  where: p.6; Fig 2a
- Agents often do not load the skills they are given.
  number: only 49% of Claude trajectories load all curated skills (curated setting), 31% with distractors. Any-skill load rate 62% (curated), 44% (retrieved), 16% (retrieved w/o curated).
  setup: as above, Claude Opus 4.6 / Claude Code
  quote: "only 49% of Claude trajectories load all curated skills in the curated setting, falling to 31% with distractors."
  where: p.6; Fig 2b
- Without curated skills, weaker models fall below their no-skill baseline, so irrelevant skills can actively hurt.
  number: Kimi K2.5 19.8 vs 21.8 no-skill. Qwen3.5-397B 19.7 vs 20.5. Claude 38.4 vs 35.4 (+3.0).
  setup: SkillsBench, retrieved w/o curated, each model in its native harness (Kimi on Terminus-2, Qwen on Qwen-Code)
  quote: "both Kimi (19.8% vs. 21.8% baseline) and Qwen (19.7% vs. 20.5% baseline) drop below their no-skill baselines, indicating that irrelevant retrieved skills can actively mislead the agent"
  where: p.7
- Harness affects load rate, and loading more does not mean performing better.
  number: Kimi loads in 86% of curated-setting trajectories vs 62% for Claude. Kimi pass rate 38.9 curated vs 38.5 force-loaded.
  quote: "indicating that skill utility involves not just loading skills but also effectively utilizing their content."
  where: p.6
- Agentic search beats direct search for finding skills. Semantic matters, keyword alone is poor.
  number: Recall@3 direct semantic 38.1 vs agentic semantic 56.8 (+18.7). Agentic keyword 24.1. Hybrid w/ content: R@5 65.5, R@10 68.3.
  setup: Claude Opus 4.6 + Claude Code, pool = 34k skills incl. curated, ground truth = SkillsBench curated skills
  quote: "With the same semantic search tool, agentic search outperforms direct search in Recall@3 by 18.7 points"
  where: p.5, Table 1
- Query-specific refinement recovers much of the lost performance. Query-agnostic gives small, inconsistent gains.
  number: Claude 40.1 to 48.2 (SkillsBench retrieved w/ curated). Qwen 26.7 to 30.8. Query-agnostic Claude 40.1 to 42.0. Terminal-Bench 2.0: +4.1 Claude, +5.6 Kimi, +4.9 Qwen. Improves 7 of 9 cases.
  setup: single refinement iteration, no ground-truth verifier. Specific = agent attempts the task, then merges skills. Agnostic = each skill refined alone via Anthropic's skill-creator with A/B tests on synthetic queries.
  quote: "Query-specific refinement improves performance in 7 out of 9 cases in Table 2. On SKILLSBENCH with curated skills in the retrieval pool, it improves Claude from 40.1% to 48.2%"
  where: p.8, Table 2
- Skill retrieval plus refinement helps on a benchmark not built for skills.
  number: Claude Opus 4.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 tasks) 57.7 to 65.5. Retrieval only 61.4. Kimi 46.6 to 56.2. Qwen 44.7 to 49.1 (retrieval alone 44.2, slightly below baseline).
  quote: "improve the pass rate from 57.7% to 65.5% with Claude Opus 4.6"
  where: p.2, p.8, Table 2
- Refinement raises load rate (descriptions and content become more usable).
  number: Claude 44% to 72% (SkillsBench w/ curated). Kimi 69.7 to 95.2.
  quote: "skill loading rates also increase substantially with query-specific refinement (e.g., 44% to 72% for Claude on SKILLSBENCH w/ curated)"
  where: p.8
- Refinement is a multiplier on existing skill quality, not a generator of new knowledge.
  number: LLM-judged coverage (1-5): SB w/ curated 4.01/3.83/3.85 (Claude/Kimi/Qwen), SB w/o curated 3.49/3.31/3.39, TB 4.02/3.96/4.08. Query-specific refinement on SB w/o curated: Claude 38.4 to 37.9, Kimi 19.8 to 23.1, Qwen 19.7 to 21.5.
  setup: judge GPT-5.4 scores the retrieved set against the task
  quote: "refinement acts more like a multiplier on existing skill quality rather than a generator of new knowledge."
  where: p.9, Table 3
- Query-specific refinement can backfire when the model misjudges which skills are useful.
  number: Kimi SkillsBench w/ curated 33.5 to 26.7
  quote: "the exploration and self-evaluation process can be counterproductive when the model misjudges which skills are useful."
  where: p.8
- Stronger models ignore bad skills better.
  quote: "stronger models can better ignore irrelevant skills, while weaker models are more likely to be hurt by low-quality retrieved skills."
  where: p.7
- Skill collection: 34,198 real skills from skillhub.club and skills.sh, MIT/Apache-2.0 only, deduplicated by content. (p.4, App. A)

LIMITS
- Only two benchmarks (SkillsBench 84 tasks after excluding 3, Terminal-Bench 2.0 89 tasks) and three models. Only 3 runs per task, and no variance or confidence intervals are reported.
- Refinement is a single iteration. Query-specific refinement costs a full exploration pass per task at inference time. Query-agnostic was applied only to the retrieved skills, not the whole 34k, because that was "cost-prohibitive".
- Kimi query-agnostic results are missing (Terminus-2 has no subagents).
- Model and harness are confounded. Each model uses its own harness, so differences cannot be split between model and harness.
- Query-specific refinement fails when relevant skills are absent (SB w/o curated). Skill-quality coverage is judged by an LLM (GPT-5.4).
- Retrieval ground truth is only the SkillsBench curated skills, so Recall@k measures curated-skill recovery, not usefulness. The search tool is a custom engine (BM25 + Qwen3-Embedding-4B, RRF k=60).
- Model names and benchmark versions date it (Opus 4.6, Kimi K2.5, Qwen3.5-397B, Claude Code v2.1.19).
- Authors name no explicit limitations section. The conclusion calls for better retrieval, offline refinement, and skill ecosystems that account for model capability.

BUILDS ON
SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026) and SWE-Skills-Bench (Han et al., 2026), which are the idealized setups it critiques. Agent Skills format (Anthropic, 2026a) and Anthropic's skill-creator meta-skill. Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026). Harbor framework (2026). Qwen3-Embedding (Zhang et al., 2025). Reciprocal Rank Fusion for hybrid search. Self-improvement lineage: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), Memento (Zhou et al., 2025), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2025), and others on skill libraries (Voyager-style, Wang et al., 2023; SkillWeaver, Zheng et al., 2025). Related skill work: SkillRouter (Zheng et al., 2026), SkillNet (Liang et al., 2026), SoK Agentic Skills (Jiang et al., 2026b).

CODE
- RRF hybrid score (App. A, p.14): "the RRF score for a skill is sum_s ws/(k+r_s), where rs is the rank in search method s, ws is the method weight (default 0.5 for both keyword and semantic), and k=60". Content-aware semantic: "(1-w)·sim_meta + w·sim_content" with w=0.05, BM25 weights name 10, description 5, content 5.
- The finding-skills skill (App. A, pp.14-16) is a SKILL.md with "When to Use", the search API, and a 4-step workflow (analyze task, search per sub-task, review and select by relevance and github_stars, record found skills). Search results return name, description, a 100-word skill_md_snippet, skill_id and github_stars.
- Query-specific refinement prompt (App. C.1, pp.17-18) has three phases (read task and skills, attempt using the skills, reflect and write refined skills). Key rule: "Compose, don't copy." Single iteration. No verifier access.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): left, a SkillsBench task whose curated skills spell out the solution (idealization). Right, pass rate bars across the five settings for 3 models. Quickest picture of the degradation.
- Fig 2 (p.6): (a) pass rates for FL/CS/CD/Rw/Ro/NS. (b) share of trajectories that load any skill or all curated skills. Shows the load-rate drop behind the pass-rate drop.
- Fig 3 (p.9): Terminal-Bench tensor-parallel task. Before refinement the agent loads one partial skill and fails at world_size 2. After refinement, a merged skill passes. Illustrates composition across skills.
I did not run the figures script, so these captions are from the extraction.

PROBLEMS
- Figure 2 bar values are scrambled in text extraction. Only numbers stated in the prose or tables are quoted above.
- Table 2 values partly run together (for example "40.1 44.433.569.7"). I split them using the prose. Check against the PDF before citing digits from that table that the prose does not repeat.
- The extraction has odd spacing in places ("ofskills", "Qwen3.5-397B") but no unreadable text.
- Source contains no embedded instructions. The prompts in appendices C and D are the paper's own data and were not followed.
- Relevance to the note: the paper supports rules 1, 2 and 5 of "Writing a skill" only indirectly. It shows descriptions and metadata drive load decisions and that refinement raises loading. It does not test negative examples, templates, or the security claim. It also does not support the note's "~10 tokens" or "few hundred tokens" cost figures. It does not measure token cost at all.
